sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Database engine and base class setup
sections.what: Decides whether to use SQLite or PostgreSQL, creates the matching connection, sets up the session factory, and creates the base class for all models.
sections.why: Makes the app work with a simple file database for easy setup or a full server for real use.
sections.watch_out: Changing the database address switches the whole app to a different database type, so existing data will not move over automatically.

sections.name: get_db
sections.title: Per-request session helper
sections.what: Hands a fresh database session to a request, then closes it when the request finishes.
sections.why: Makes sure each request has its own session and that connections are not left open.
sections.watch_out: Any changes not committed before the request ends are lost.

sections.name: init_db
sections.title: Table creation helper
sections.what: Creates every table known to the base class in the connected database.
sections.why: Used by setup scripts to build tables on a new database.
sections.watch_out: It does not change existing tables, so schema changes need a separate migration.

summary: Creates the database connection for the app, the session factory that starts each database conversation, and the base class all models inherit from.
purpose: Provides the one connection point the rest of the app uses to read and write data.
why: Likely reason: every database action needs a connection, and creating it in one place keeps the settings consistent.
how: It checks whether the database address starts with sqlite. For SQLite it uses a single shared connection that allows several threads. For PostgreSQL it uses the default pool, or no pool when the environment is testing. It then builds a session factory and a base class. The get_db helper hands out one session per request and closes it afterwards. The init_db helper creates all tables.
inputs: The database address from the settings.
outputs: A database engine, a session factory, a base class for models, and the get_db and init_db helpers.
risks: Sessions are not committed automatically, so forgetting to commit will lose changes. init_db is not called on startup in main.py, so tables must be created another way.
debug: If the app cannot connect, check the database address and that the database is running. If data does not save, confirm the code commits its session. If a table is missing, run the table creation step.
